displayQuote: When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe

meta.title: Who really said "When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. John Muir wrote it in My First Summer in the Sierra (Houghton Mifflin, 1911), p. 211 — the July 27 entry. The popular "tugs" version is a fake.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: John Muir, My First Summer in the Sierra (1911), page 211. But the widely shared "tug on anything in nature" wording is not his.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page. The sentence appears in Muir’s My First Summer in the Sierra (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1911), page 211, in the entry dated July 27 in Chapter VI, “Mount Hoffman and Lake Tenaya.” One caution: the first edition prints a lowercase “universe,” not the capital “Universe” that circulates online.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: My First Summer in the Sierra
Chapter VI, “Mount Hoffman and Lake Tenaya” — the entry dated July 27
Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company, 1911 (copyright page: “Published June”) — page 211
Muir’s journals of his 1869 summer in the Sierra Nevada

source.excerpt: No Sierra landscape that I have seen holds anything truly dead or dull, or any trace of what in manufactories is called rubbish or waste; everything is perfectly clean and pure and full of divine lessons. This quick, inevitable interest attaching to everything seems marvelous until the hand of God becomes visible; then it seems reasonable that what interests Him may well interest us. When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe. One fancies a heart like our own must be beating in every crystal and cell, and we feel like stopping to speak to the plants and animals as friendly fellow-mountaineers.
trail: The sentence sits in the July 27 entry of Chapter VI in the Sierra Club’s online text ↗, and in Project Gutenberg’s full text of the book ↗.
We then checked it against the printed page: the Internet Archive scan of the 1911 Houghton Mifflin edition ↗ carries the line on page 211, set with a lowercase “universe.”
Quote Investigator ↗ cites the same edition and the same page 211, describing the 1911 book as based on Muir’s travels in 1869.
The far more common “tug on anything” wordings are listed as paraphrases by Wikiquote ↗ and rejected outright by the Sierra Club ↗.

author.name: John Muir
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: John Muir was a Scottish-born American naturalist, author and environmental philosopher, described in his own century as a botanist, zoologist and glaciologist, and remembered chiefly as an early advocate for preserving wilderness in the United States. In the summer of 1869 he went into California’s Sierra Nevada with a flock of sheep and kept the journals that would sit unpublished for decades. He worked them up into My First Summer in the Sierra, published in 1911 — the book that carries this sentence.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Muir. What goes wrong is the wording. A rewritten version circulates far more widely than the sentence he actually published, and the underlying idea is routinely credited to him as though he thought of it first.

items.who: “When one tugs at a single thing in nature, he finds it attached to the rest of the world.”
items.why: The Sierra Club’s John Muir Exhibit runs a standing Misquote Alert ↗ on this one, stating flatly that “Muir never used the word ‘tugs’ when writing about the interconnections of things.” Wikiquote likewise files the “tug” wordings under Misattributed ↗ as paraphrases.

items.who: “Tug on anything in nature and you will find it is connected to everything else.”
items.why: The Sierra Club ↗ says the earliest source it could find for the “tugs” misquote through a Google Books search is Judi Bari’s Timber Wars (Common Courage Press, 1994), page 130 — decades after Muir’s book, and after his death.
The capitalised “Universe” is how the line is almost always shared, and how Wikiquote ↗ prints it. The 1911 first edition ↗ sets it lowercase: “everything else in the universe.”

items.who: Muir as the originator of “everything is connected”
items.why: The phrasing is his; the thought is not new with him. Quote Investigator ↗ traces written expressions of the notion back through Gotthold Ephraim Lessing in 1769 and Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. in 1896, and says the idea “probably occurred in the mind of a primordial philosopher.”

misattribution.truthLine: What Muir actually published, on page 211 of the 1911 first edition ↗: “When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Muir wrote the line into a book about a working summer, not a manifesto. He had gone up into the Sierra Nevada in 1869 tagging along with a flock of sheep, and the passage that carries this sentence is mostly weather and water — snowmelt, streams “singing bank-full,” pot-holes, boulder dams. The famous clause arrives almost as an aside, one observation among many.

That is why it travels so well. It is a plain sentence about how nothing in a landscape stands alone, written decades before it saw print, and it has since been adopted as a shorthand for ecological thinking — often quoted as though Muir had invented the idea rather than phrased it memorably.
context.detailsSummary: On the gap between the 1869 summer and the 1911 book
detailsBody: Muir’s Sierra summer was 1869; My First Summer in the Sierra was published by Houghton Mifflin in 1911, its copyright page marked simply “Published June.” Quote Investigator describes the book as based on his travels in 1869.

The Sierra Club’s John Muir Exhibit, citing Stephen Fox’s John Muir and His Legacy (page 291), reports that the corresponding journal entry for July 27, 1869 put the thought differently: “When we try to pick out anything by itself we find that it is bound fast by a thousand invisible cords that cannot be broken, to everything in the universe.” The Sierra Club treats both the journal wording and the published “hitched” wording as authentic Muir.
